searchText: With the decision of bi-weekly EOF meetings, we do not have any scheduled call for today. Just updated the protocol calendar to avoid confusion. EOF Implementers Call #53 is scheduled for July 10th. Feel free to add [agenda](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/1085) items. I got a question since we are failing an EOF header test which I do not understand. The spec says the maximum number of container sections is 0x00FF. However, since the container section size itself has to start at the number 1 (by spec), does this mean that if I want to encode 255 (0xFF) container sections, I am actually allowed to use container section size 0x0100? The test which we fail has 0x0100 container sections, and it is marked to pass (we fail). (So, in the container bytecode it has 0x0100 encoded) By EIP 3540 this is not allowed though > container section size itself has to start at the number 1 (by spec) I don't think that's the case, EOFCREATE[0] and RETURNCONRACT[0] are very common stanzas in EEST. EIP 3540 I think the "number of container sections" is confused here with "container section size". the "number of container sections" follows the sub-containers section kind (03) which is optional. So we want to avoid `03 0000` combination because `03` is optional. So we will never see RETURNCONTRACT[255]? I understand the 03 0000 thing, but the spec says that 03 0100 is not allowed 03 0001 means one container, starting at index 0 And I assumed the containers are zero-indexed so There is an EOF container test which is marked to be valid, but it has 03 0100 in it Ah, ok I see what you mean. Maybe the spec should say `0x0001–0x0100`. And then `RETURNCONTRACT[255]` works. I think so, yes But I think then it should also note that the containers are zero-indexed because everything else in the spec is 1-indexed evmone has `CONTAINER_SECTION_NUMBER_LIMIT = 256` 😉 We have limit 255 😦 I'll change 🙂 Should I open an issue for the spec? Or I can just open a quick PR also Yes, how you prefer. this, a little further down in the spec the maximum numbers of code/container sections are 1024 and 256 resp. (inclusive). The table is off > - the number of code sections must be greater than `0` and not exceed `1024` ... > - the number of container sections must not exceed `256`. The number of container sections may not be `0`, if declared in the header I think the table mixes the theoretical ranges for 2-bytes integer with logical ones implied by the validation rules. Also the bullet points below duplicate the rules regarding admissible values from the table. Maybe we should fix the values in the table to logical ones (e.g. 0x0001-0x0100 for num containers) and remove the duplicate rules from the bullet points. https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/8719 https://github.com/ipsilon/eof/pull/141 I just opened two prs 🙂 If you want I can also remove those duplicate ones (but I think they are nice there, as a reminder for the reader) no worries, I can play with this and see which option is the cleanest When thinking about it, I think this option is the most consistent, since num code sections is also not 0-based (need at least one code section). So it makes sense to ban 0x03 0000 0x030000 is banned Ah right sorry I thought you meant that, but you mean the bullet points yea I just mean layout and editing, and whether or not to duplicate the values BTW, I have a question about the description of the stack validation with `min_stack_value` and `max_stack_value`. Is there any scenario where those two values are not equal? yup, offhand, so it might be off somewhat: ` ... RJUMPI[1] PUSH0 NOP`. Here at `NOP` you either PUSH0-ed or not, depending on the RJUMPI condition. Ahhh right of course But then does this section in mega EOF not need to get updated to use the same terms? ``` Otherwise instruction was already visited (by previously seen forward jump). Update this instruction's recorded stack height bounds so that they contain the bounds computed in 2.3, i.e. target_stack_min = min(target_stack_min, current_stack_min) and target_stack_max = max(target_stack_max, current_stack_max), where (target_stack_min, target_stack_max) are successor bounds and (current_stack_min, current_stack_max) are bounds computed in 2.3. ``` It seem to use both `min_stack_value` and `target_stack_min` I'm assuming after seeing your argument that those vars are the same 🙂 But I'm now just thinking out loud, can't you now not via a circular argument reason that you can create a body which stack overflows? 🤔 Oh wait we still check for overflows but not underflows R-right? in runtime we only check overflow on CALLF/JUMPF, and there you can overflow. in eof validation you can detect under and overflow, that is, such code won't pass validation (should not 😅 ) What if I try to deploy code to RJUMP to myself? I'm sure I'm missing something obvious in the stack validation thing though 😅 you mean `PUSH0 RJUMP[-4]` ? Yes something like that > 3. If the successor is reached via backwards jump, **check** if the recorded stack height bounds equal the value computed in 2.3. Validation fails if they are not equal, i.e. we see backwards jump to a different stack height. in other words, jumping backwards ~~min_stack_height == max_stack_height~~ stack height bounds must be exactly the same for all "ways" to reach the destination, otherwise validation error I see yes sorry scratch that, fixing fixed now. In the `NOP PUSH0 RJUMP[-4]` when you're reaching the PUSH0 from the NOP, you're one stack item less compared to when you're backwards RJUMPing. Yes so min stack height / max stack height for that nop would both be 0, but for the backwards jump is 1, so this invalidates it? correct I see Now I have to convince myself that this works 🙂 BTW, the text in the stack validation (which you just copied) does not match what mega eof says, I think that one is correct? (it does need the terminology update since it talks about the target_stack_min and not stack_height_min there) 😅 `RJUMP[-3]` jumps on itself (therefore valid). the `RJUMP[-4]` is invalid. yea, I never remember this, fixing so the previous example is off too, it is RJUMPI[1] that jumps over the next instruction if condition is satisfied. Fixed in the example too Thanks 🙂 Yeah I got the idea from the description 👍 So just for my understanding, these min_stack and max_stack height divergences only happen on conditional jumps - right? So the only candidates here are RJUMPI and RJUMPV ? And the design intent from the compilers is you would jump into a divergent section that would then revert/return/stop and exit. So the differing heights don't get in the way of CALLF as you are jumping out of the current message frame Otherwise you have duplicate terminal runs that differ only in validated stack height. Or a bunch of swaps and pops before them. Should have followed a compiler course at some point I think, but this does all make sense 🙂 Ok I think I just convinced myself that this works I was about to ask about underflows but realize that this is indeed also captured by same argument How should I call the error when these stack heights diverge? "Unstable stack"? 😆 Quick question, are there stack validation tests already in the EOF tests? I have not implemented this algorithm, and the tests which I am currently failing does not seem to have to do with stack validation, except with some JUMPF/CALLF stuff (release 1.0.5 of tests) EEST produces EOF tests, and 4200 tests from ethereum/tests have been ported in. I'm not aware of any gaps (doesn't mean there aren't any) 5450 tests I think you mean? Oh, jumpf. I was still in jump mode. 6206 for jumpf. 3540 for callf callf tests could be re-homed, but coverage should be the same. I don't think there is a test which would invalidate code such as `NOP PUSH0 RJUMP[-4]` currently So for calls to other code sections the stack validation does seem to be there, but not for stack validation in the code section itself So the `min_stack_size` `max_stack_size` forward/backward jump stack check algorithm What about https://github.com/ethereum/execution-spec-tests/blob/a3743c807eacce14fe9d147a3414578d082171f9/tests/prague/eip7692_eof_v1/eip3540_eof_v1/code_validation_jump.py#L592 and https://github.com/ethereum/execution-spec-tests/blob/a3743c807eacce14fe9d147a3414578d082171f9/tests/prague/eip7692_eof_v1/eip3540_eof_v1/code_validation_jump.py#L444 ? In that case I don't think they are in the latest release of the fixtures We do not fail that test and I definitely do not have this stack check I'm not sure if that one is referenced in the tests filled, need to update those tests and put them in the appropriate test functions let me open a PR Are you running eofTests or just state tests and blockchain tests? Bad containers only really show up in the EOF tests. EOFTests The bad containers start to show up in the blockchain tests also now I think, since the tx-eof-create EIP just got added to the release it seems 🙂 Not sure if it has invalid eof containers though Also I'm not sure if there is any SWAPN stack check tests yet, but these also do not seem to be there 🙂 We have no stack rules for that opcode and we do not fail any there
